title: Thank-You Notes
short: Write soon, name the gift or kindness, say how you will use or enjoy it, add a personal line, and close warmly; a handwritten note is still the warmest.
trouble: Learners think an email or text never counts, or that a note sent late is worse than none. A late note is always better than no note.

blocks.html: You learned the parts of a thank-you note years ago. As an adult you will write them for gifts, dinners, interviews, help in hard times and favors at work. The shape stays the same; the occasions grow.
Write soon. Name the gift or kindness, say how you will use or enjoy it, add a personal line, and close warmly. A handwritten note is still the warmest thanks.

A gift or favor took someone's time, thought or money. A note closes the circle: it tells the giver that the kindness arrived and mattered. Naming the specific gift and how you will use it proves you noticed; a vague "thanks for the gift" could have been written without opening the box. Handwriting takes a few minutes, and the reader can feel that.

blocks.name: et-note

parts.thanks: Thank you so much for the cookbook you sent for my new apartment.
parts.detail: I made the lentil soup on page 40 on Sunday, and my roommates asked for seconds.
parts.personal: I hope you will come for dinner soon so I can cook for you.

blocks.cap: A thank-you note with its parts tagged.

blocks.title: After a dinner party
blocks.q: Sam had dinner at Priya's home on Saturday. What might his note say?
steps: Thanks, named: "Thank you for the wonderful dinner on Saturday."
Detail: "Your lemon tart was the best I've had, and I loved meeting your sister."
blocks.a: A short note that names the dinner and something specific about it.

blocks.title: A late note
blocks.q: Leo got a graduation gift from his uncle two months ago and never wrote. Is it too late?
steps: A late note is always better than no note.
He writes it now, with a light apology: "I'm sorry this is so late."
Then he thanks his uncle as warmly as he would have in June.

blocks.html: Thinking an email or text never counts, or that a note sent late is worse than none. A handwritten note is warmest, a prompt email or text is far better than silence, and a late note is always better than no note.
